title: Not Abandoned, and a Servant Who Endures
overview: The LORD answers the claim that he walked away from his people, and then a faithful servant describes taking abuse while trusting God to clear his name.

parts.label: No divorce papers (v. 1)
parts.note: In that world a man could send his wife away with a written certificate, and a parent in debt could sell children to a creditor. The LORD challenges the exiles to show such papers: their exile came from their own wrongs, not from God casting them off for good or paying a debt.

parts.label: Not too weak to rescue (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: A 'short arm' was a picture of weakness, and God insists his is not short, even though no one answered when he called. Drying up the sea and leaving fish to rot recalls the escape from Egypt, and covering the sky in sackcloth, a rough cloth worn in mourning, means making it dark.

parts.label: Taught every morning (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: A new speaker, usually called the servant, says God wakes him each morning like a teacher rousing a student, so he can give tired people words that hold them up. Scholars are unsure who he is: the prophet himself, faithful Israel, or a figure still to come.

parts.label: Beaten but not backing down (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: He lets himself be beaten, has his beard torn out (a deep humiliation then), and is spat on, yet sets his face 'like flint' because he trusts God to help him. Christians have long read this in light of the beating and spitting Jesus endured before his death.

parts.label: Let the accuser step forward (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The language comes from a courtroom: God, who will clear his name, is close by, so the servant dares anyone to bring a charge. His opponents will wear out like old clothes eaten by moths.

parts.label: Darkness or homemade fire (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: Anyone walking in the dark is urged to trust the LORD, while those who light their own torches are told to walk by that light and will end up lying down in pain. Many read the torches as relying on one's own plans instead of God, though the image is open to interpretation.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the servant here speaks directly and only about Jesus, or first about the prophet or faithful Israel in Isaiah's own day, with Jesus seen later as the fullest fulfillment.
think: Is there a difference between enduring mistreatment with steady resolve and simply putting up with it, and where would you draw that line?
